extracted.intended_audience: members of the Royal Society, natural philosophers, physicians, anatomists, and observational scientists (17th-century audience)
extracted.subtask_description: Compilation of 17th‑century natural history observations, book reviews, anatomical reports, and astronomical notices intended to communicate empirical findings, classifications, and corrective comments to fellow natural philosophers. Emphasis is on observational rigor, documentation, and comparison with prior authorities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relevance to contemporary practitioners
rubrics_metrics.description: Upon the subjects here enumerated this author has no observations that can interest the physicians of the present days.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Book reports / scientific communications should contain observations or results that are of use or interest to the active practitioners in the field; absence of such makes the work less noteworthy for the intended professional readership.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quality and accuracy of illustrations
rubrics_metrics.description: the distinction ... is made very clear by the neat and accurate cuts annexed
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrations (cuts/plates) should be neat and accurate and serve to clarify distinctions and morphological details described in the text; good plates strengthen arguments about form and structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experimental demonstration with reputable witnesses
rubrics_metrics.description: he affirms, to have done it actually in the presence of Signor Magalotti, and Monsieur Thevenot, two very intelligent and cautious persons
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims of experimental demonstration should be performed transparently and, when possible, in the presence of credible witnesses to bolster credibility and allow independent verification of extraordinary observations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clear classification and discriminating ranks
rubrics_metrics.description: reduces all changes of insects ... into four classes or ranks; which are discriminated by four different ways of production, change and growth
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Taxonomic and classificatory works should offer clear, discriminating categories based on distinct modes of production or development; provide definitions and examples for each class to make the system usable and testable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acknowledge exceptions and limits
rubrics_metrics.description: some few excepted, which he acknowledges he does not yet well understand
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors should openly acknowledge phenomena or cases they cannot yet explain rather than over-claiming; explicit acknowledgement of limits strengthens trustworthiness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compare claims against earlier authorities and literature
rubrics_metrics.description: he affirms that Moufet and others do err ... that Harvey mistakes ... that Goedart errs ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When advancing novel interpretations or corrections, situate arguments with respect to prior authors, identify specific disagreements, and justify why established views are mistaken or incomplete.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide precise positional and measurement data for astronomical claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Its longitude is now 1° 52' 10" in Aquarius, and lat. 47° 15' 21" ... Ascensio recta ... Declinatio Borealis ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reports of new stars or celestial objects must include precise coordinates (longitude/latitude or RA/declination), magnitude estimates, and measured distances from known stars so others can locate and verify the object.

rubrics_metrics.name: Demonstrate absence of object in prior observations/catalogues
rubrics_metrics.description: there can be no doubt that this is completely a new star, and not visible in the year 1660. For in the years 1659, 1660, 1661, it happened that I made observations ... but I found no star of the third magnitude in that place
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To claim discovery, show that prior careful observations and catalogues (e.g., Bayer's Uranometria) lack the object in the claimed position or magnitude; document your prior searches and comparisons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Repeated observations and temporal monitoring
rubrics_metrics.description: It however wonderfully decreased in the month of September, so that by the 14th of October it could not be observed at all
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Track brightness and position over time; report temporal changes to distinguish transient phenomena from fixed objects and to characterize variability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use and report of adequate instruments and comparative instrument notes
rubrics_metrics.description: The telescope of 50 feet long ... The former writes ... observed Saturn with his telescope of 22 feet ... The telescope ... showed the face of Saturn very distinctly
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State the instruments used (aperture/length) and, when possible, compare observations with those obtained using different instruments to assess instrument-dependent effects and to corroborate findings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Test observational hypotheses by conformity with predicted appearance
rubrics_metrics.description: saw his figure to be quite conformable to what it should be according to his hypothesis; viz. the ansae or arms to be very narrow
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observations should be used to test theoretical hypotheses; report whether the observed phenomena conform to predictions (e.g., ring orientation/appearance) and note deviations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide thorough descriptive detail and physical evidence for extraordinary natural events
rubrics_metrics.description: a most terrible flash of lightning, and a fearful thunder-clap, which lighted down ... causing such a hideous crack, fire-flash, smoke and damp there, as if many fire balls had been thrown down ... leaving a bad sulphureous smell behind
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Narratives of unusual events should include detailed descriptions of physical effects (damage, smells, sounds), locations struck, condition of objects, and behaviour of people present to allow assessment and possible causal inference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Record injuries, damages and their specific particulars
rubrics_metrics.description: Eight persons only were hurt : ... one had the upper back part of his cloth-coat, as also his shirt and skin somewhat torn; ... the waistcoat being edged with a small silver lace, the lace was smutted almost every where
rubrics_metrics.guidance: List specific observed injuries and material damages with as much detail as possible (clothing, wounds, pierced holes, scorched areas) to build an evidentiary record rather than vague claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Detailed dissection with measurements and organ descriptions
rubrics_metrics.description: we first weighed this birth; the weight whereof was eight pounds and a quarter; the circumference of the left head was about eleven inches ... We found one navel vein, and one liver ... there were two urinary bladders, two wombs, four kidneys
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anatomical reports should include weights, circumferences, lengths, counts of organs, and careful morphological descriptions; report anomalies and how they interconnect to support functional inferences (e.g., nourishment pathways).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of manipulative tests to probe function
rubrics_metrics.description: we could not follow it with the probe, but doubting a failure in that experiment, we made an essay with a blow pipe, and thereby we found, that the wind would go no further than the place above-mentioned
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When possible, perform simple manipulative experiments (probing, blowing, injecting) to test anatomical connections or functional hypotheses, and report methods and limitations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide specimens/provenance for verification and replication
rubrics_metrics.description: a piece of old willow wood being sent me from Sir John Barnhard from Northamptonshire, was produced before the Society
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When reporting observational or specimen-based claims, indicate provenance and make specimens available to peers (or deposit in collections) so others can inspect, repeat, or extend the observations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Detailed description of ecological/behavioral context and construction
rubrics_metrics.description: many insects curiously wrapt up in green leaves, in several channels or burrows, each with 12, 14, or 16 leaves round the body, and several of them with as many little round bits of leaves at each end, to stop them up close
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describe nesting/construction behaviours, counts (e.g., number of leaves), spatial arrangement (direct/sideways burrows), and morphology of constructions to enable others to recognize and compare similar cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attempt rearing / controlled observation of life history stages
rubrics_metrics.description: Some of these maggots I took out of their theca or bag, and put them in warm places in the sun; ... then I took one of them out of the wood, and opened the leaves, and felt something stir, hearing also a humming noise like that of a bee; and ... a perfect bee flew out
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Attempt to rear immature forms under controlled conditions and record outcomes (growth, metamorphosis, death). Report environmental conditions and handling that may affect survival to interpret observed life histories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Share specimens and observations for collaborative inquiry
rubrics_metrics.description: I desire one of the bees, because all mine being of a late hatch ... I fear I shall not see their last metamorphosis this year. ... if you please to send me Dr. King's account, and one of your bees, I may perhaps add something
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage exchange of specimens and detailed accounts between observers to allow cross-verification, broader sampling, and collective progress in documenting species' life cycles.
